## Profile
- Headline: Strategy and operations leader across consumer tech and management consulting: marketplace growth, subscription and pricing economics, and competitive strategy, working AI-first.
- Career thread: I moved from advising on strategy (NRI Consulting, 2018–2023), to the operator's seat in a fast-moving marketplace (Uber Eats ANZ Strategy & Planning, 2023–2026), to regional consumer strategy across five APAC markets (2026–present). Throughout, I've turned messy questions that span many teams into decisions people can act on, and been strict about what the evidence actually shows.
- Strength: Geo and growth strategy for marketplaces: deciding where to invest and running the cross-functional program behind it (cards: C20, C06, C09, C25)
- Strength: Competitive response: reading competitor moves quickly and turning them into proportionate, measured responses (cards: C23, C45, C26, C02)
- Strength: Subscription and pricing economics: price-and-benefit changes, offer design and measurement that waits for real renewals (cards: C33, C30, C34, C36, C81)
- Strength: Hands-on, AI-first analytics: governed SQL dashboards, simulators and executive documents built with AI coding tools (cards: C80, C83, C22, C30)
- Strength: Consulting rigour: market entry, go-to-market and due diligence for multinational and public-sector clients (cards: C50, C51, C59, C55, C64)
- How I work with AI: Daily, and central to how I work. I use Claude Code, Cursor and Codex to write and review SQL, build data pipelines, dashboards and simulators, and publish analysis as commentable web pages. I keep a personal agent workflow for daily planning and meeting prep, and wrote a reusable playbook and skill for executive-ready documents.
- Tools: SQL (Presto/Hive), Google Sheets and Excel modelling, Python, R, VBA, BI dashboards, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, React/TypeScript (AI-assisted), Experiment design

## C20 — Growing Uber Eats in underserved regional areas of Australia and New Zealand
- Rank: 1
- Period: 2024-03 to 2026-05
- Role: Uber Eats — ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: Australia, New Zealand
- Tags: Uber · ANZ · Marketplace · Strategy · Project management
- Relevant to: Strategy & Ops, BizOps, Consulting
- Skills: geo strategy, prioritisation frameworks, working-group leadership, performance tracking
- Tools: Google Sheets modelling, SQL specification
- Headline: Led the strategy workstream for a seven-function program to grow Uber Eats in underserved regional Australia and New Zealand; the country GM approved the plan and regional category position rose about 24 points in a year.
- Context: Growth was uneven, and regional areas lagged metro on restaurant choice and competitive position.
- Problem: Turn a broad 'grow regional' ambition into a ranked city list with entry rules that five teams could act on, without reducing it to one number, and keep it current as the market changed.
- What I did:
  - Set the entry rules: Designed city-prioritisation criteria combining merchant coverage, trip potential and competitive position, then applied them to about 30 priority cities and 34 second-tier cities in Australia, and 12 priority cities in New Zealand.
  - Re-plan when the market moves: When Menulog announced its exit in November 2025, widened the plan from 15 to about 30 priority cities to include places where Uber Eats wasn't yet leading, and pushed back on an over-broad New Zealand proposal, narrowing it to 12 cities.
  - Give each tier its levers: Matched each city tier to specific levers (sales coverage, consumer offers, delivery reliability and speed standards), so each team knew what it owned.
  - Run one shared tracker: Wrote the fortnightly working-group pack for Acquisition, Consumer, Marketplace, Marketing and Merchant Ops, and built the city-level tracker the group worked from.
- Artifacts: Prioritisation framework, revised annual plan, project plan, city and area tracker, working-group packs.
- Outcome (adopted): The country GM approved the plan in November 2025 and it became a named growth priority in the 2026 annual plan. Regional Australia category position rose about 24 percentage points year on year, regional trips grew about 50%, active stores in priority areas grew about 35%, and restaurant selection against the nearest competitor went from parity to about 1.35x (program results, shared with Acquisition, Consumer and Marketplace; includes the lift from Menulog's exit). After handover, priority cities kept outgrowing other regional cities on bookings and share (<redacted>).
- What I learned: Explicit entry criteria and staged decisions keep multi-team investment debates grounded when evidence is incomplete. A plan also needs a trigger for re-planning, not just a start date.
- Related: C09, C25, C14, C23

## C23 — Preparing for and responding to Menulog's exit from Australia
- Rank: 2
- Period: 2024-08 to 2026-05
- Role: Uber Eats — ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: Australia
- Tags: Uber · ANZ · Marketplace · Strategy · Execution · Project management
- Relevant to: Strategy & Ops, BizOps, Chief of Staff
- Skills: scenario planning, response playbooks, cross-functional governance, retrospective analysis
- Tools: Google Sheets, SQL specification
- Headline: Wrote the response playbook months before Menulog's exit from Australia and ran governance across six functions; offers launched within 48 hours, and Uber Eats captured the large majority of the share Menulog left.
- Context: A major competitor's exit was possible, and a slow or uncoordinated response would hand its customers and restaurants to others.
- Problem: Six functions each had their own levers and timelines. The response had to be ready before the announcement, move within days, and be judged on solid evidence afterwards.
- What I did:
  - Prepare before the news: Wrote the response playbook months ahead and ran a pre-exit sprint with two drills, so teams knew their offers, owners and triggers in advance.
  - Launch within 48 hours: When Menulog announced its exit in November 2025, coordinated Consumer, Acquisition, Merchant Ops, Marketing, Marketplace and Product so offers went live within 48 hours.
  - Run one dated tracker: Kept a dated tracker separating our actions from market changes, with written assumptions, so teams worked from one picture instead of competing stories.
  - Review what really worked: Ran a look-back review across the response to separate what drove the gains from what just happened at the same time.
- Artifacts: Response playbook, drill materials, dated response tracker, summary decks, look-back review.
- Outcome (launched): Uber Eats captured the large majority of the share Menulog left. Regional Australia category position rose about 11 percentage points in five weeks, and weekly first-time restaurants, customers and couriers rose 30–50% (shared results across six functions).
- What I learned: The response was fast because the decisions were made before the event. A disciplined tracker and an honest look-back turn one-off firefighting into a reusable playbook.
- Related: C20, C45, C26

## C33 — Rolling out Uber One price and benefit changes in Japan and Taiwan
- Rank: 3
- Period: 2026-06 to 2026-09
- Role: Uber — APAC Consumer Strategy
- Markets: Japan, Taiwan
- Tags: Uber · APAC · Marketplace · Subscriptions & loyalty · Measurement · Execution
- Relevant to: Growth & Monetization, Product Ops, Strategy & Ops
- Skills: pricing change governance, cohort measurement design, launch readiness, cross-market synthesis
- Headline: Co-wrote the global playbook for Uber One price-and-benefit changes and applied it to the public Japan and Taiwan changes; the full Japan member base moved over on the planned date with no operational incident.
- Context: Uber One prices and benefits changed in Taiwan and then Japan in 2026 (public changes). The region needed a repeatable way to run these changes and to judge whether they worked.
- Problem: Announcement reactions, new sign-ups and renewals by existing members all happen at different times, so early numbers can look healthy before renewals come due. Each change also involved several product, legal, localisation and web teams, with different customer groups switching on different dates.
- What I did:
  - Codify the change playbook: Co-wrote the global playbook for membership price changes with two regional colleagues, covering communications timing, ownership, annual-plan treatment, test users and go/no-go checks. Carried the lessons from Taiwan into Japan's readiness checks.
  - Measure at the renewal point: Set measurement rules that kept notices, opt-outs, new sign-ups, active and passive cancellations and renewal-based retention separate, measured annual plans on their own, and labelled cohorts whose renewals hadn't happened yet as 'not yet due', not as lost.
  - Run the page like a launch: Owned the Japan public Uber One page update: mapped the review chain (product, legal, localisation, web operations), the cutover timing and the pre-publish checks, and kept 'configured' separate from 'seen working in production'.
  - Write the regional read-out: Wrote the regional impact memo (13 findings across acquisition, opt-outs, churn, engagement and economics), proposed a price-setting framework for the next markets, and briefed regional leadership.
- Artifacts: Global price-change playbook, regional impact memo, measurement definitions, public-page review map and launch checklists.
- Outcome (launched): The full Japan member base moved to the new price on the planned date with no operational incident, and Japan's pre-launch tests, built from the playbook, caught a plan defect before customers saw it. Detailed retention and economics results: <redacted>.
- What I learned: Measure customers at the point they actually renew, and treat a price change as a launch with named owners, live evidence and a rollback plan. Announcement-week numbers aren't a retention result.
- Related: C30, C36

## C06 — Diagnosing growth by city, category and brand
- Rank: 4
- Period: 2023-09 to 2026-05
- Role: Uber Eats — ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: Australia, New Zealand
- Tags: Uber · ANZ · Marketplace · Analysis · Strategy
- Relevant to: Strategy & Ops, BizOps, Consulting
- Skills: market diagnosis, segmentation, competitive analysis, executive Q&A
- Tools: SQL specification, Google Sheets modelling
- Headline: Led city and category share deep dives for Uber Eats ANZ, including a Sydney diagnosis that moved the team from broad promotions to targeted offers for new, infrequent and lapsed customers.
- Context: Growth was uneven across cities, categories and brands, and market averages couldn't explain why.
- Problem: Find where results really differed and which causes could be fixed, keeping what the data showed separate from guesses about cause.
- What I did:
  - Break the average apart: Led share deep dives for Sydney, Christchurch and New Zealand, splitting movements by customer segment, membership, category and competitor activity.
  - Answer the exec question fast: Built a de-duplicated view of category users that explained to senior leaders why category growth and Uber Eats growth diverged.
  - Check brands on equal terms: Set up brand-level checks using the same measures and periods for every brand, including a switching analysis of a national restaurant chain's exclusive delivery deal.
  - Hand findings to the right owner: Passed local follow-ups to the teams with context, and contributed analysis to a New Zealand share response led by the New Zealand strategy lead.
- Artifacts: Diagnostic decks, analysis workbooks, brand briefs, market briefs and prioritisation notes.
- Outcome (adopted): The Sydney diagnosis moved the city from 'monitor' to 'act': Consumer launched targeted $0 delivery-fee offers, quests and promotions for new, low-frequency and lapsed customers in July 2025, followed by a targeted delivery-fee test.
- What I learned: Good diagnosis depends on the right level of detail: broad enough to see shared patterns, specific enough to find the cause you can actually act on.
- Related: C02, C20, C26

## C80 — Building the APAC consumer dashboard end to end with AI
- Rank: 5
- Period: 2026-09 to present
- Role: Uber — APAC Consumer Strategy
- Markets: Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Taiwan, Sri Lanka
- Tags: Uber · APAC · Marketplace · Subscriptions & loyalty · Analysis · Execution
- Relevant to: BizOps, Strategy & Ops, Product Ops
- Skills: metric governance, data reconciliation, dashboard design, AI-assisted engineering
- Tools: SQL (Presto/Hive), Python, Claude Code, git and pull-request review
- Headline: Built a single consumer dashboard for five APAC markets end to end with AI-assisted coding: about 108 governed metrics, daily refresh and AI-drafted weekly commentary, live within about four weeks of plan.
- Context: Global and market reports didn't give one comparable regional view of consumers, so performance discussions started from different numbers.
- Problem: The dashboard had to be trusted. Every metric had to tie back to finance and business-review definitions, refresh reliably, and be maintainable by one person.
- What I did:
  - Write the source of truth: Wrote about 19 governed SQL queries (Presto/Hive, window functions, grouping sets, chunked backfills) covering active eaters, trips per user, lifecycle, membership, promotions and finance, all reviewed through pull requests.
  - Ship it, then iterate: Built the app, daily job and validation checks with Claude Code as a pair. It went from mock-up to live on real data in about four weeks, followed by about 120 pull requests of improvements.
  - Reconcile before you publish: Checked numbers against finance tables, the business-review sheets and a peer team's metric catalogue, fixed our own queries, and flagged upstream issues to their owners until settled months tied to finance reporting.
  - Automate the commentary: Added an AI-drafted weekly commentary section at the regional operations head's request, with a human check before it's shared.
- Artifacts: Live dashboard, governed query library, validation checks, metric definitions and weekly commentary.
- Outcome (launched): Launched to 21 regional leaders and market leads, with 20 users in the first five weeks and 70% coming back. Its cohort data fed the regional capital-allocation review. It aims to be the business-review reference, but no forum is confirmed to run on it yet.
- What I learned: With AI as a pair, one person can build and maintain production-grade analytics, but only if every number is reconciled to a second source before anyone sees it.
- Related: C47, C81, C82

## C02 — Rebuilding the ANZ market-intelligence report and tracking
- Rank: 6
- Period: 2023-08 to 2026-05
- Role: Uber Eats — ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: Australia, New Zealand
- Tags: Uber · ANZ · Marketplace · Research · Analysis
- Relevant to: Strategy & Ops, BizOps, Consulting
- Skills: research synthesis, metric governance, narrative development, signal-vs-noise rules
- Tools: Google Sheets, SQL specification, scripted data refresh
- Headline: Rebuilt and ran the monthly ANZ market-intelligence report for about 2.5 years as a single source of truth for leadership, and created a margin-of-error rule the global strategy team adopted.
- Context: Market news and competitive data came from many places, and leaders needed one dependable monthly picture instead of scattered updates.
- Problem: The report had to stay short and comparable month to month, avoid over-reacting to noisy share data, and keep running when people moved on.
- What I did:
  - Make one source of truth: Rebuilt the monthly report around a fixed set of measures (category share, app downloads, fees, restaurant selection, satisfaction, brand spend, reliability and offers), with an analyst refreshing the data by script and me writing the commentary.
  - Separate signal from noise: Created a margin-of-error rule: act on a share change only when it exceeds the error band and persists for two periods.
  - Keep a memory of the market: Ran a weekly promotions tracker and regular review meetings, and wrote data definitions and source notes so trackers didn't depend on anyone's memory.
  - Publish on a fixed rhythm: Published to the ANZ leadership team and senior leads across departments around the same date each month, then handed the report over with a written guide.
- Artifacts: Monthly reports and decks, weekly promotions tracker, data dictionaries, review notes, handover guide.
- Outcome (adopted): The report ran monthly for about 2.5 years and informed consumer fee changes, supply-versus-demand investment in Sydney and Melbourne, and a buy-now-pay-later payment launch. The margin-of-error rule was written into the global strategy team's guidelines for reading share data, and my competitor-response framework was picked up by other markets.
- What I learned: Regular reports help decisions when they answer the same key questions each time and say how confident they are. A clear rule for what counts as a real change prevents a lot of wasted reaction.
- Related: C06, C11, C21, C22, C01

## C47 — Setting up the APAC Consumer Strategy role
- Rank: 7
- Period: 2026-09 to present
- Role: Uber — APAC Consumer Strategy
- Markets: Multi-market
- Tags: Uber · APAC · Marketplace · Strategy · Project management
- Relevant to: Strategy & Ops, Chief of Staff
- Skills: role design, operating-model design, decision-rights mapping, metric governance
- Headline: Defined a new regional consumer strategy role from scratch (scope, decision rights, mission, three pillars and key results) and saw it adopted in the regional consumer plan.
- Context: After a September 2026 reorganisation I stepped into a newly created regional consumer strategy role, the first of its kind for the APAC team.
- Problem: The role was deliberately broad. It had to be clear where the regional team coordinates, where it provides tools and methods, and where pricing, membership, market and product teams stay in charge.
- What I did:
  - Learn from other regions: Compared how similar roles worked in the global, US and Canada, EMEA, Latin America and ANZ teams before drafting a scope proposal.
  - Map who decides what: Wrote what the role would and wouldn't own, using a decision-rights framework, with input rights on fees and membership pricing and partners in consumer, pricing, marketplace, membership and strategy teams.
  - Set mission and key results: Drafted the mission, three pillars and key results (monthly active eaters and trips per user) with my manager, plus a step-by-step plan to consult and build.
- Artifacts: Role scope proposal, decision-rights outline, mission and pillars, key results and a consult-and-build plan.
- Outcome (adopted): The role, its mission and three pillars were adopted in the regional consumer plan, and I'm named the regional driver for the consumer dashboard and consumer home page work.
- What I learned: Agree who decides and how metrics are defined before investing in the build. A coordination role earns its place by giving teams tools, not by taking decisions from them.
- Related: C80, C81, C16

## C45 — Responding proportionately to McDonald's $0.99 delivery promotion
- Rank: 8
- Period: 2026-03 to 2026-05
- Role: Uber Eats — ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: Australia
- Tags: Uber · ANZ · Marketplace · Subscriptions & loyalty · Analysis · Measurement · Strategy
- Relevant to: Strategy & Ops, Growth & Monetization, BizOps
- Skills: cohort segmentation, scenario framing, monitoring design, targeting
- Tools: SQL (Presto/Hive), experiment design (control and placebo groups)
- Headline: Co-wrote the response to McDonald's $0.99 delivery promotion in Australia: segmented exposed customers, recommended a targeted membership trial over a broad fee cut, and set trigger-based monitoring.
- Context: McDonald's launched a $0.99 delivery fee on its own channel in 2026, and leaders wanted to know how exposed Uber Eats customers were and how hard to respond.
- Problem: Tell real competitive pressure apart from normal ups and downs, and avoid an expensive broad response that the evidence didn't justify.
- What I did:
  - Find who is exposed: Segmented customers by membership, McDonald's loyalty and Uber Eats order frequency to find which groups were most at risk.
  - Target instead of blanket: Recommended a 6-month Uber One trial for high-loyalty, high-frequency non-members rather than a broad $0 delivery fee.
  - Set trigger points: Built monitoring with control and placebo groups, and held the broad fee cut behind a clear trigger instead of launching it pre-emptively.
  - Write it for the GM: Co-wrote the response deck for the country GM with the McDonald's account team.
- Artifacts: Customer segmentation, scenario model, monitoring plan with triggers, leadership deck.
- Outcome (launched): The targeted trial went live, the trigger-based monitoring ran as designed, and the broad fee cut was never needed.
- What I learned: A credible response doesn't have to be immediate or broad. Uptake of the trial came in far below the full-uptake assumption in my cost model, so I now model opt-in explicitly.
- Related: C23, C07

## C28 — Consolidating regional membership priorities for annual planning
- Rank: 9
- Period: 2026-06 to 2026-09
- Role: Uber — APAC Consumer Strategy
- Markets: Multi-market
- Tags: Uber · APAC · Marketplace · Subscriptions & loyalty · Strategy · Project management
- Relevant to: Product Ops, Strategy & Ops, Chief of Staff
- Skills: portfolio prioritisation, roadmap governance, cross-market synthesis, operating-rhythm design
- Headline: Consolidated 8 market membership requests into 7 regional product asks across 5 APAC markets for annual planning; 4 of the 7 were funded or part-funded in the following year's product plan.
- Context: As regional membership product champion, I had to bring market requests, product dependencies and planning deadlines into one view before the regional leadership planning deadline.
- Problem: Markets described their needs in different levels of detail and with different assumptions about timing, ownership and evidence. The roadmap had to show what was committed, blocked or only proposed without looking more settled than it was.
- What I did:
  - Put every ask in one format: Collected requests from Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Taiwan and Sri Lanka in a common format (customer problem, decision needed, dependencies, maturity, owner) and merged 8 market asks into 7 regional asks.
  - Write the priorities memo: Wrote the regional membership priorities memo for leadership planning, backed by about ten research pages, and filed the planning intake and benefit-change timeline.
  - Run decision-focused reviews: Supported a recurring product and operations sync built around decisions, dependencies and launches, with pre-reads, named owners and a decision log; recorded open disagreements instead of forcing consensus.
- Artifacts: Regional priorities memo, market ask register, planning intake, benefit-change timeline and decision log.
- Outcome (adopted): At the product funding review, 4 of the 7 regional asks were funded or part-funded in the following year's product plan. I held the regional view until membership moved to a separate team in the September reorganisation and handed it over.
- What I learned: Alignment doesn't mean agreeing on everything. It means being clear on what's known, what's disputed and who decides next, and showing uncertainty openly rather than hiding it in a polished list.
- Related: C39, C30

## C30 — Modelling the economics of a tiered membership and member benefits
- Rank: 10
- Period: 2026-06 to 2026-10
- Role: Uber — APAC Consumer Strategy
- Markets: Multi-market
- Tags: Uber · APAC · Marketplace · Subscriptions & loyalty · Analysis · Strategy
- Relevant to: Growth & Monetization, Strategy & Ops, Product Ops
- Skills: benefit economics, budget simulation, cost-control design, concept localisation, executive briefing
- Tools: React/TypeScript, Claude Code, SQL (Presto/Hive), Google Sheets modelling
- Headline: Led the regional workstream on a tiered-membership concept for an APAC market and built the budget simulator myself with AI; it became the working budget tool in weekly cross-functional reviews, though the concept was not launched.
- Context: A globally designed member-reward and tier idea needed adapting to an APAC market where members behave differently and the economics differ, and new benefits had to be paid for without simply adding cost.
- Problem: Borrowed settings from another market wouldn't hold. A per-order benefit risked concentrating cost on already-loyal heavy users, and the design had to stay workable if the full product experience slipped.
- What I did:
  - Build the simulator myself: Built an interactive budget simulator with AI-assisted coding (React/TypeScript, 15 versions with automated checks) on real local trip data, with member groups, qualifying thresholds and expected usage instead of borrowed assumptions.
  - Cap the heavy-user risk: Showed where cost concentrates and laid out the product options: caps, delayed eligibility, minimum order conditions, and funding new benefits by reallocating existing member discount spend rather than adding to it.
  - Make the economics visible: Built a membership economics dashboard covering five markets from finance data, and showed gaps between data sources rather than forcing one answer.
  - Brief the decision makers: Ran the weekly regional sync with product operations, the global membership team and the market team, and wrote the executive briefing on launch dependencies, legal requirements and a fallback using existing tools.
- Artifacts: Budget simulator, membership economics dashboard, cost-sensitivity tables, assumptions list and an executive launch briefing.
- Outcome (not launched): The simulator became the working budget tool in the weekly cross-functional reviews, and the cost-control options were costed side by side for the decision. The concept was not launched.
- What I learned: Reusing an idea across markets means reusing the modelling approach, not the numbers. A design that's cost-neutral on paper still needs a funding owner before it's real.
- Related: C33, C28

## C50 — Battery-swapping market entry strategy in India for a Japan-based multinational
- Rank: 11
- Period: 2018 to 2023
- Role: NRI India — Automotive Industry Consulting
- Markets: India, Southeast Asia
- Tags: NRI · India · Southeast Asia · Automotive · Energy · Strategy · Research
- Relevant to: Consulting, Strategy & Ops, Growth & Monetization
- Skills: market sizing, consumer research, pricing and sales strategy, partnership development, go-to-market planning
- Tools: Excel modelling
- Headline: Built the India market-entry strategy for a Japan-based multinational's EV battery-swapping business, from consumer surveys in 10+ cities to an entry plan for 40+ cities and partnership talks with 50+ firms.
- Context: A Japan-based multinational wanted to know whether battery-as-a-service (riders swap or subscribe to batteries instead of buying them) could become a real business in India.
- Problem: The strategy had to tie together demand, customer needs, pricing, operations and partners. A single adoption forecast wasn't enough, and the model hadn't been proven at scale in India.
- What I did:
  - Size it city by city: Ran consumer research with surveys across 10+ cities, and built market, feasibility and profitability models by customer segment.
  - Turn research into choices: Compared business-model assumptions and turned them into decisions on target customers, pricing, sales strategy and a phased entry plan covering 40+ cities.
  - Line up the partners: Facilitated partnership discussions with CXOs of 50+ leading private and public-sector firms to secure the partners the model depended on.
  - Lead a two-tier team: Led a two-tier team of consultants through the research, modelling and recommendation work.
- Artifacts: Market and city models, survey findings, commercial scenarios, a phased entry plan and a partner pipeline.
- Outcome (delivered): Delivered the entry strategy and city roll-out plan, which led into a multi-stakeholder pilot (C51) that enabled the client's launch. The client's projected revenue from the business: <redacted>.
- What I learned: Test business-model assumptions against how things actually run. A promising technology needs a clear customer use and a believable path to repeat revenue.
- Related: C51, C79, C73

## C25 — Adopting hexagon-based area clusters as ANZ's planning layer
- Rank: 12
- Period: 2024-10 to 2026-05
- Role: Uber Eats — ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: Australia, New Zealand
- Tags: Uber · ANZ · Marketplace · Analysis · Strategy
- Relevant to: Strategy & Ops, Product Ops
- Skills: spatial analysis, analytical methodology, rollout leadership, cross-functional adoption
- Tools: Google Sheets, SQL specification, governed data tables
- Headline: Led ANZ's adoption of the global team's hexagon-based area clusters, the first international market to do so, and built the rules-based layer that tagged every area for targeting and planning.
- Context: City-level planning was too coarse, and the global team had built an algorithm that grouped small hexagons into delivery areas.
- Problem: The algorithm was global. ANZ needed it adopted quickly, made understandable to local teams, and linked to how they define and compare areas.
- What I did:
  - Be the first adopter: Ran ANZ's feedback round and rollout with the global strategy team, regional operations and local operations; it went live in July 2025.
  - Add a tactical layer: Built a rules-based grouping on top, comparing reliability, merchant coverage and share against medians, and refreshed it each quarter as governed tables.
  - Give each area a posture: Tagged every Australia and New Zealand area with a strategic posture, from 'build the experience' to 'defend share'.
  - Explain it plainly: Explained the logic in plain terms to strategy and operations colleagues.
- Artifacts: Method document, tactical grouping tables, explainer deck, progress updates.
- Outcome (adopted): The clusters became ANZ's base geographic layer, used to select priority areas, set sales territories, target delivery-fee offers and run the regional growth tracker, across Acquisition, Marketplace, Consumer and performance marketing. The global team built the clustering algorithm, not me.
- What I learned: Adopting a global method fast needs a local translation layer and plain explanations, not just the algorithm.
- Related: C20, C09

## C09 — Building ANZ's city strategy dashboards and tracker
- Rank: 13
- Period: 2023-09 to 2026-05
- Role: Uber Eats — ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: Australia, New Zealand
- Tags: Uber · ANZ · Marketplace · Analysis · Execution
- Relevant to: BizOps, Strategy & Ops, Product Ops
- Skills: dashboard design, metric specification, data reconciliation, geographic analysis
- Tools: Google Sheets, SQL specification, AI-assisted dashboard building
- Headline: Designed and maintained ANZ's city and area performance dashboards, which became the single source of truth for a seven-function growth working group and the monthly business review.
- Context: Broad market strategy didn't give teams the local evidence they needed for city-level choices, or a shared base to revisit them.
- Problem: Teams needed one trusted city and area view, with definitions everyone accepted and numbers that matched reference data.
- What I did:
  - Specify what matters: Designed the city and area tracker, monthly category-share dashboards and priority-city views, and specified every metric.
  - Build the front end: Built the Google Sheets layer myself while offshore analysts wrote and refreshed the SQL.
  - Reconcile before publishing: Checked analyst outputs against reference data and fixed definition errors before numbers reached leaders.
  - Wire it into the rhythm: Fed priority-city data into the fortnightly working group and the monthly business review.
- Artifacts: Dashboards, city and area tracker, maps, metric definitions, planning decks.
- Outcome (adopted): In April 2026 the working group agreed all teams would work from this tracker as the single source of truth. My successor carried it into the second half of 2026, and the priority-city mapping moved to a governed data table.
- What I learned: A dashboard earns trust through reconciled numbers and stable definitions, not through more charts.
- Related: C20, C25, C21

## C22 — Bringing AI into market-intelligence reporting
- Rank: 14
- Period: 2024-10 to 2026-05

## C81 — Diagnosing consumer pricing and promotion effectiveness across APAC
- Rank: 15
- Period: 2026-10 to present
- Role: Uber — APAC Consumer Strategy
- Markets: Multi-market
- Tags: Uber · APAC · Marketplace · Analysis · Strategy
- Relevant to: Growth & Monetization, Strategy & Ops, BizOps
- Skills: pricing analysis, promotion effectiveness, cohort strategy, scenario simulation, executive storytelling
- Tools: SQL (Presto/Hive), Claude Code, React/TypeScript
- Headline: Led a set of hands-on pricing and promotion diagnostics across five APAC markets: what drives active eaters and frequency, whether fee changes hurt growth, and whether promo spend reaches the intended customers.
- Context: Regional leadership asked what was holding back active eaters and trips per user, and whether fees and promotions were working as intended.
- Problem: Fee and promo decisions are owned by pricing and market teams, so the work had to inform them without duplicating their analyses. Pricing effects are also confounded by the wider economy and overlapping changes.
- What I did:
  - Find the growth drivers: Analysed 24 months of monthly active eaters and trips per user across five markets, broken down by customer cohort and membership, and turned it into a 37-slide executive brief.
  - Test whether pricing hurts: Reviewed the effect of fee changes and member fee benefits in two markets using same-customer panels, reconciled to the consumer dashboard (22-slide review).
  - Follow the promo money: Compared where fee and promotion spend actually goes by customer cohort against the global strategy's intent, and built a start-of-month promotion spend workbook for regional leadership.
  - Propose a cohort plan: Built a margin-neutral lever simulator for one market and a cohort-level fee and promotion plan (10 cohorts, 15 months, interactive explorer) for market teams to react to.
- Artifacts: Executive briefs, a pricing-impact review, a lever simulator, a cohort plan explorer and a promotion spend workbook.
- Outcome (in progress): In progress: the analyses feed the market teams' monthly pricing and promotion reviews and next year's plans, but no pricing decision is traced to them yet.
- What I learned: In a coordination role, the fastest path to impact is pre-wiring the decision owners and filling their gaps, not publishing a parallel answer.
- Related: C80, C82, C83

## C83 — An executive-ready analysis playbook and AI deck-quality guide
- Rank: 16
- Period: 2026-10 to 2026-11
- Role: Uber — APAC Consumer Strategy
- Markets: Multi-market
- Tags: Uber · APAC · Marketplace · Execution
- Relevant to: Strategy & Ops, Chief of Staff, Consulting
- Skills: AI workflow design, executive communication, quality control, knowledge sharing
- Tools: Claude Code, Python, custom Claude skill
- Headline: Wrote a playbook for turning exploratory analysis into executive documents with AI (12 rules, an 8-step process, a starter kit, a reusable Claude skill and a 12-check quality gate), now used across my own executive work.
- Context: A colleague asked how to get better executive-quality output from Claude, and my own analyses needed a repeatable way to go from exploration to a clear executive story.
- Problem: AI makes it easy to produce lots of slides quickly. The hard part is one message per slide, figures that trace back to a source, and the right depth for each reader.
- What I did:
  - Write the deck rules: Published an AI deck-quality guide with chart and slide rules, a colour palette and reusable chart-style code.
  - Codify the process: Turned the method behind a 37-slide executive brief into a playbook: 12 rules, an 8-step process, a starter kit and a reusable Claude skill.
  - Gate every figure: Added a 12-check quality gate, including tracing every figure to its source and writing at 30-second, 3-minute and 30-minute depths.
- Artifacts: AI deck-quality guide, executive-ready playbook, starter kit, reusable Claude skill and a quality checklist.
- Outcome (delivered): I've applied it to my executive briefs, the quarterly newsletter, the cohort plan and a 44-slide deck where all 178 figures traced to a source. The colleague who asked rated both highly, but wider team adoption isn't proven yet.
- What I learned: AI speeds up the drafting; the value is in the rules that make the output trustworthy and easy for executives to read.

## C01 — Running the consumer satisfaction program and rationalising research vendors
- Rank: 18
- Period: 2023-08 to 2025-05
- Role: Uber Eats — ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: Australia, New Zealand
- Tags: Uber · ANZ · Marketplace · Research · Measurement
- Relevant to: BizOps, Strategy & Ops
- Skills: survey management, vendor management, contract negotiation, measurement governance
- Tools: Google Sheets, survey tools
- Headline: Ran the monthly ANZ consumer satisfaction survey, then rationalised the research vendors: ended two contracts and cut another's cost by about two-thirds while keeping the data teams relied on.
- Context: Leadership wanted a consistent monthly read of consumer satisfaction, and the team was paying several research vendors for overlapping data.
- Problem: A headline score on its own explains little, and a stock-take showed some of the data was noisy and not clearly used, costing about three hours a week to run.
- What I did:
  - Run the monthly read: Owned the monthly satisfaction report from my first weeks: a general-population survey of about 2,000 respondents, monthly question updates, and commentary for the ANZ leadership team and senior leads.
  - Improve the instrument: Added pickup and New Zealand respondents, wrote an FAQ and definitions, and proposed linking the affordability goal to the fee-perception drivers in the survey.
  - Cut what isn't used: After a stock-take, ended two survey contracts whose data was noisy or unused.
  - Renegotiate what is: Renegotiated a data contract to about a third of its previous cost while keeping the delivery-time data teams depended on.
- Artifacts: Monthly satisfaction reports, questionnaire and definitions, vendor stock-take, renegotiated contract.
- Outcome (delivered): Annual research spend fell by <redacted>, with two contracts ended and one cut by about two-thirds, without losing data teams used. I found no evidence that a specific decision changed because of the survey itself.
- What I learned: Satisfaction programs work best when they stay consistent but are regularly asked to justify their cost. A stock-take of what is actually used is often the fastest way to save money.
- Related: C02, C03, C12

- Headline: Ran a six-month battery-swap pilot for electric three-wheelers end to end, leading a five-person PMO across eight domestic and international partners; the pilot enabled the client's business launch.
- Context: The battery-swapping entry strategy (C50) needed real-world proof. Vehicles, batteries, swap stations and daily operations had to work together on the road before the client committed to launch.

- Artifacts: Pilot plan, operations and issue trackers, partner updates, operating-review decks and a final report.
- Outcome (launched): The pilot ran to completion and enabled the client's business launch. Pilot budget: <redacted>.

## C39 — Coordinating which APAC markets join global membership features and tests
- Rank: 23
- Period: 2026-06 to 2026-10
- Role: Uber — APAC Consumer Strategy
- Markets: Multi-market
- Tags: Uber · APAC · Marketplace · Subscriptions & loyalty · Strategy · Execution
- Relevant to: Product Ops, Strategy & Ops
- Skills: opt-in governance, experiment readiness, requirements writing, capacity planning, stakeholder coordination
- Tools: Google Sheets modelling
- Headline: As the region's membership product point of contact, I took each global membership feature and test to five APAC markets with a recommendation and logged a clear yes or no from each.
- Context: Global teams designed member features, benefits and reward challenges, and each APAC market needed a clear, evidence-based decision on whether to take part.
- Problem: Markets differ in demand, commercial setup, regulation and ability to run tests that give clean answers, so one regional decision would have been wrong. Overlapping campaigns and late-loading audiences could also spoil comparison groups.
- What I did:
  - Recommend, then log the call: Took each global test to the market leads in Australia and New Zealand, Japan, Taiwan and Sri Lanka with a recommendation based on country-level results, fit, cost tolerance and clashing changes, and logged each opt-in or opt-out. Product teams designed the tests.
  - Protect the comparison groups: Asked for clean control groups, first-exposure dates and clear rules for which campaign takes priority before results were read, and kept modelled estimates separate from real results.
  - Turn manual work into requirements: Wrote product and measurement requirements for scaling partner-funded member offers (configuration, offer mapping, an incrementality standard) and backed the request for standard campaign spend tracking.
  - Plan verification capacity: Built a demand and capacity forecast for student-membership eligibility checks, with growth and decline scenarios, and managed capacity top-ups until handover.
- Artifacts: Market-fit tables, opt-in decision log, partner-offer requirements, a verification capacity tracker and forecast.
- Outcome (delivered): Every global test in the period had a recorded decision from each of the five markets, made on local evidence rather than a blanket regional call. The tracking tools that later shipped were built by product teams, not me.
- What I learned: A cheap test isn't automatically useful, and a local win doesn't prove something works across a whole market. Decide the reading rules before the test starts.
- Related: C28, C36, C34

## C36 — Bringing a global member-retention test to APAC markets
- Rank: 24
- Period: 2026-06 to 2026-09
- Role: Uber — APAC Consumer Strategy
- Markets: Japan, Taiwan, Sri Lanka
- Tags: Uber · APAC · Marketplace · Subscriptions & loyalty · Measurement · Strategy
- Relevant to: Growth & Monetization, Product Ops
- Skills: retention strategy, experiment readiness, measurement discipline, rollout coordination
- Headline: Carried a global cancellation-offer test into Japan, Taiwan and Sri Lanka and set the rule that an opt-out isn't churn until renewal cohorts mature; all three markets were recommended to keep the winning offer.
- Context: Retention was a top priority in mid-2026, and members who signalled they'd cancel needed a better response than one standard discount.
- Problem: One rescue offer hides real differences between plan types and preferences, and results can't be trusted until the setup is proven and there's a valid control group. The test itself was designed and run by global product teams.
- What I did:
  - Bring markets into the test: Shared the interim read with the regional team and asked the Taiwan and Sri Lanka teams to opt in to the global cancellation-offer test, alongside Japan.
  - Separate saying from leaving: Kept members who said they'd cancel separate from members who actually left, and insisted opt-outs weren't counted as churn until renewal-aligned cohorts had matured.
  - Track win-back honestly: Measured win-back among opt-outs after the Taiwan price change (<redacted>), labelled it observational because there was no control group, and checked approved designs against what was really live.
- Artifacts: Interim read-out, market opt-in requests, measurement notes in the price-change memo.
- Outcome (delivered): The global read-out recommended keeping the winning cancellation offer in all three markets I brought in (lift: <redacted>). I can't claim my nudge drove those market decisions.
- What I learned: Prove the setup is complete and the control group is valid before claiming members were won back, and define precisely who qualifies for a win-back offer.
- Related: C33, C34

## C34 — Reviewing membership sign-up offers: trial length and annual plans
- Rank: 25
- Period: 2026-06 to 2026-09
- Role: Uber — APAC Consumer Strategy
- Markets: Multi-market
- Tags: Uber · APAC · Marketplace · Subscriptions & loyalty · Analysis · Strategy
- Relevant to: Growth & Monetization, Strategy & Ops
- Skills: offer portfolio analysis, cohort segmentation, decision framing
- Tools: SQL (Presto/Hive)
- Headline: Contributed the analysis behind a review of extended free trials in one market and a five-market evidence pack on annual plans, recommending offers by customer history rather than one blanket cap.
- Context: Sign-up offers needed to be judged on how many people became paying members, not just how many signed up.
- Problem: Longer free access boosts sign-ups but delays finding out who will pay, and promotion-driven demand had to be separated from demand for the plan itself. The offer decisions sat with the market and global membership teams.
- What I did:
  - Split the decision by cohort: Recommended against a blanket cap on trial length: remove the longest trials from the least-retentive never-member and inactive cohorts, use short trials for lapsed paying members, and test a short trial followed by discounted months.
  - Check live offers against intent: Compared what was live with what was intended and flagged out-of-date long-trial campaigns that were still running.
  - Build the annual-plan evidence: Built a five-market evidence pack on plan mix, continuation, engagement and pre-sign-up frequency, recommending monthly as the entry plan with an upgrade offer once members had seen value.
- Artifacts: Trial-length review, five-market annual-plan evidence pack, decision tables by customer group.
- Outcome (delivered): The out-of-date long-trial campaigns I flagged were later switched off, and the market owner shortened the longest trials for low-frequency segments. Those decisions were theirs, and I can't trace them directly to my work.
- What I learned: Agree the main goal before tuning how long an offer lasts. Total members, paying members and long-term value can point to different answers at the same time.
- Related: C36, C39

- Relevant to: Strategy & Ops, Consulting

- Headline: Ran regular benchmarking of comparable companies' public results for ANZ leadership, separating comparable trends from metrics that only looked alike.
- Context: Comparable businesses published regular results, a useful but scattered view of how they were changing.
- Problem: Different companies define their public numbers differently, so comparisons had to be careful not to treat unlike metrics as the same.
- What I did:
  - Check definitions first: Checked source quality, definitions and time periods before comparing anything.
  - Compare trends, not rankings: Compared broad trends and wrote down where comparisons held and where they broke down.
  - Translate for leaders: Turned technical disclosures into short takeaways for internal discussion.
- Artifacts: Benchmarking notes, comparison tables, leadership summaries.
- Outcome (adopted): The team got a repeatable, careful way to discuss comparable businesses' public results alongside the monthly market report.
- What I learned: The most useful benchmark is often not a ranking but a clear view of where comparisons hold and where they break down.
- Related: C02

## C49 — Comparing competitor research across APAC markets
- Rank: 34
- Period: 2026-07 to 2026-09
- Role: Uber — APAC Consumer Strategy
- Markets: Multi-market
- Tags: Uber · APAC · Marketplace · Subscriptions & loyalty · Research · Strategy
- Relevant to: Strategy & Ops, Consulting
- Skills: research maturity assessment, source evaluation, taxonomy design, prioritisation
- Tools: Google Sheets modelling
- Headline: Built a side-by-side view of competitor research across five APAC markets, showing what existed, how reliable and recent it was, and what to improve first.
- Context: I wanted to know how well competitor research could support consumer and membership decisions in each market across the region.
- Problem: Markets had different research sources, definitions, update frequencies and quality. Missing information couldn't be treated as proof that nothing existed.
- What I did:
  - Set a common taxonomy: Defined a shared list of research types and put every market's inputs into the same format.
  - Grade evidence, not markets: Separated what was confirmed from what was only reported or unclear, and noted how fresh and reliable each source was instead of giving a single rating.
  - Rank the gaps: Grouped related items and built a view of which gaps to close first, keeping local detail visible while making the comparison easy to scan.
- Artifacts: Cross-market comparison table, source quality list, shared categories and a priority list.
- Outcome (delivered): Regional and market teams had one shared starting point for discussing research gaps and where to invest.
- What I learned: A useful maturity view shows how good and how recent the evidence is, not just a score.

## C12 — Measuring consumer affordability
- Rank: 35
- Period: 2023-11 to 2026-04
- Role: Uber Eats — ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: Australia, New Zealand
- Tags: Uber · ANZ · Marketplace · Measurement · Research
- Relevant to: Growth & Monetization, Strategy & Ops
- Skills: measurement design, model framing, research synthesis
- Headline: Designed a transparent way to measure what customers actually pay across order types, splitting price into its parts so teams could debate affordability on evidence.
- Context: Teams needed a clearer way to talk about what customers actually pay across different kinds of orders.
- Problem: Affordability isn't one displayed price. It depends on what people order, fees, promotions and what they compare against, and all of these change.
- What I did:
  - Break price into parts: Defined a measure that splits the price experience into menu price, fees and promotions.
  - Test it over time: Checked whether comparisons still made sense across periods and situations.
  - Explain the model plainly: Explained the assumptions in plain language so people could question them instead of treating the index as a black box.
- Artifacts: Measurement model, method explainers, research notes, review summaries.
- Outcome (adopted): The team got a reusable, transparent way to discuss consumer value, which fed the satisfaction program and leadership planning discussions.
- What I learned: Affordability measures are more useful when their assumptions are visible and they can answer several different questions.
- Related: C13, C01, C24

## C44 — Reading fuel-cost signals for consumer behaviour
- Rank: 36
- Period: 2026-03 to 2026-05
- Role: Uber Eats — ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: Australia, New Zealand
- Tags: Uber · ANZ · Marketplace · Research · Analysis
- Relevant to: Strategy & Ops, Consulting
- Skills: hypothesis framing, signal interpretation, research synthesis
- Headline: Contributed a note turning rising fuel prices into testable hypotheses about consumer behaviour across rides and delivery, with alternative explanations built in.
- Context: Fuel prices were changing, and people asked how consumers might change their behaviour across rides and delivery.
- Problem: It was tempting to read cause into coincidence, so the news had to become careful questions instead.
- What I did:
  - List the mechanisms: Reviewed the fuel-price trend and listed the ways consumers might plausibly respond.
  - Split now from later: Separated what we could observe right away from what needed deeper checking.
  - Build in alternatives: Treated other explanations as part of the analysis and kept the questions testable against our own data.
- Artifacts: Research note and fuel-price signal tracker.
- Outcome (delivered): Leaders got a structured set of questions to test, instead of a headline assumption.
- What I learned: Big economic trends are good prompts but weak conclusions. Spell out the mechanism, list other explanations and decide what evidence would change your mind.
- Related: C12, C24

- Problem: The technologies differed in maturity, cost, use, demand and competition, so no single performance measure could rank them fairly.
- What I did:
  - Set fair criteria: Defined practical and commercial criteria that worked across technologies at different stages.
  - Assess each option: Assessed each technology on maturity, cost, use cases, demand and competition.
  - Rank what to pursue: Built a prioritisation matrix of which technologies to investigate further.
- Artifacts: A technology landscape, evaluation criteria, a prioritisation matrix and a research deck.
- Outcome (delivered): Delivered the technology landscape and a prioritised shortlist for the R&D team's next phase.
- What I learned: Spell out assumptions about maturity and commercial readiness when comparing technologies at different stages.
- Related: C73, C79

## C03 — Reviewing the scope of my strategy role
- Rank: 60
- Period: 2023-09 to 2024-03

- Markets: Australia, New Zealand
- Tags: Uber · ANZ · Marketplace · Strategy · Project management
- Relevant to: Chief of Staff, Strategy & Ops
- Skills: scope mapping, portfolio prioritisation, stakeholder communication
- Tools: Google Sheets
- Headline: Mapped my broad strategy and planning remit into workstreams six months in, which led to stock-takes of the market report and survey program that later cut vendor spend.
- Context: My strategy and planning work had grown broad, and I needed a clear picture of what I was responsible for.
- Problem: Explain a varied set of work without reducing it to a task list, and see where time was going versus where value was.
- What I did:
  - Group work into themes: Grouped my work into long-running workstreams and mapped the regular meetings and deliverables behind each.
  - Separate reactive from strategic: Compared short-term requests with ongoing responsibilities to show where time was scattered.
  - Stock-take the big recurring items: Ran stock-takes of the monthly market report and the satisfaction survey, covering time spent, use and data quality.
- Artifacts: Scope deck, work tracker, stock-takes of recurring reports.
- Outcome (delivered): The review made expectations easier to discuss with my manager and set up the stock-takes that led to rebuilding the market report and rationalising research vendors.
- What I learned: Reviewing your scope from time to time is a practical tool, not just a look back. It separates reactive from strategic work and makes prioritising and handover easier.

## C13 — Comparing menu and in-store prices
- Rank: 61
- Period: 2023-12 to 2025-03
- Role: Uber Eats — ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: Australia, New Zealand
- Tags: Uber · ANZ · Marketplace · Measurement · Research
- Relevant to: Strategy & Ops, Consulting
- Skills: measurement design, data comparability, research operations
- Headline: Designed a repeatable method for comparing delivery menu prices with in-store prices across ANZ, with explicit matching rules and caveats.
- Context: Strategy teams needed a consistent way to compare prices on delivery menus with prices in store.
- Problem: Prices were collected through different channels, formats and times. The hard part was comparing them consistently.
- What I did:
  - Define what's comparable: Set matching rules for which observations could be compared, with written exclusions and caveats.
  - Organise repeat collection: Built a collection template and tracker for repeated data gathering.
  - Keep facts and reading apart: Kept observed price differences separate from interpretation so people knew what the method could and couldn't show.
- Artifacts: Measurement framework, collection template, tracker, research note.
- Outcome (delivered): The team could discuss relative pricing without false precision, and the method fed the wider affordability measure.
- What I learned: Price comparisons are most credible when the matching rules, timing and handling of missing data are spelled out.
- Related: C12

## C52 — Field research on how drivers use connected-car services
- Rank: 63
- Period: 2019
- Role: NRI India — Automotive Industry Consulting
- Markets: India
- Tags: NRI · India · Automotive · Research
- Relevant to: Consulting, Product Ops
- Skills: qualitative research, ethnography, customer-journey synthesis, insight translation
- Headline: Helped design and run ethnographic field research into how Indian drivers use their vehicles and digital services, turning observation and interviews into concrete service-design questions for a car maker.
- Context: A car maker wanted new connected-car features grounded in how drivers actually live with their vehicles.
- Problem: Feature ideas needed to rest on drivers' real motivations, habits and frustrations, which usual product assumptions could miss. The sample was small, so findings had to be framed carefully.
- What I did:
  - Observe, then ask: Helped design research that combined observing drivers in daily use with in-depth interviews.
  - Organise by behaviour: Grouped findings around behaviours, attitudes and unmet needs rather than by feature.
  - Hand over questions, not answers: Turned what we heard into service-design questions to test, while being clear about the limits of a small sample.
- Artifacts: Interview guides, fieldwork summaries, customer journey maps and insight decks.
- Outcome (delivered): Delivered journey maps and insight decks that reframed the questions the product team was asking about connected services.
- What I learned: This kind of research is most useful when it changes the questions a product team asks. It should spark ideas to test, not stand in for the whole market.
- Related: C53, C58
